NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The question-answered sentence first: Install a pulsed flow diverter system using existing valves and pumps to periodically reverse flow direction and velocity profile through the heat exchanger channels. Standard practice uses fixed flow direction and relies on periodic mechanical cleaning; this intervention introduces periodic flow reversal and velocity pulses to disrupt biofilm and scale formation through shear stress and particle scouring, without chemical treatment. Adjacent-technique clearance: The closest existing practice is chemical dosing or ultrasonic cleaning; this is different because it uses only hydraulic perturbation via existing infrastructure. The mechanism attacks the failure's driving physics (biofilm adhesion and scale nucleation) by applying transient shear forces and flow profile changes that dislodge incipient deposits.

PHYSICS CHECK — Governing physical relation: Biofilm shear stress τ = μ(du/dy), where μ is dynamic viscosity and du/dy is velocity gradient. Flow reversal and pulsing increase peak du/dy by 3-5× locally at channel walls. Magnitude verification: For district cooling water (μ ≈ 0.001 Pa·s), a pulse from 0.5 m/s to 2.0 m/s increases τ from 0.5 Pa to 2.0 Pa, exceeding the adhesion strength of most biofilms (<1 Pa). This reduces the net deposition rate by >80% per pulse cycle, sustaining heat transfer coefficient above 2500 W/m²K.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — (Standard practice: mechanical cleaning every 3-6 months; no flow modification)
- (a) Existing PLC controller (uses existing logic module)
- (b) Standard 3-way ball valve, DN50 PN16 (installed on heat exchanger inlet line)
- (b) Standard centrifugal pump, 5 m³/h, 3 bar (installed on recirculation line)
- (c) Operating procedure: "Set PLC to trigger valve/pulse cycle every 24 hours: 2 minutes reverse flow at 1.5 m/s, 5 minutes forward flow at 2.0 m/s"
- (c) Configuration change: "Route pump output to heat exchanger inlet via 3-way valve during pulse cycles"

- Installation: 0 labor (uses existing valves/pump); standard practice: 8 labor-hours for cleaning
- Commissioning: 2 labor-hours (PLC programming); standard practice: 8 labor-hours for cleaning
- Operation: 0 additional energy (pulse cycles use existing pump capacity); standard practice: 0 energy
- Maintenance: 0 additional (no new consumables); standard practice: 4 labor-hours per cleaning
- Operational loss: 0 (pulses occur during low-load periods); standard practice: 8 hours downtime per cleaning
- Conclusion: Same burden class (labor/energy/downtime reduced or equal)

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Install flow meters and pressure transducers on heat exchanger inlet/outlet; record heat transfer coefficient weekly for 12 months. Instruments: Existing temperature sensors + portable flow meter. Pass/fail threshold: Heat transfer coefficient remains >2500 W/m²K for 12 months without exceeding 0.5 ppm chlorination. Duration: 12 months. Kill criterion: Coefficient drops below 2500 W/m²K at any inspection.
